In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of a membrane-intercalation proteoglycan, named CPGIIIB, which mediates the interaction of a tumor cell with its surrounding interstitial matrix.
the isolation and characterization of a membrane-intercalation proteoglycan with a capacity to mediate interaction between tumor cells and interstitia matrix.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CPG proteoglycan family of membrane-intercalated hybrid proteoglycants is a novel family of cell surface proteoglycands that mediate the cell-matrix interactions in a variety of cell types.

the CPGIIB proteoglycane, which is a membrane-intercalate hybrid proteoglycana, is a membrane-intercalcated proteoglyean with heparan sulfate chain that mediates the interaction of tumor cells with the interstitial matrix via the fibronectin receptor.
CPGIIIA, CPGIIIB, and CPGIIIC proteoglycants were isolated from the cell layer of the P29 clone of Lewis lung carcinoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CPG proteoglycan family is composed of at least three species, CPGIIIB, CPGIIIM, and CPGIIIT, which are all membrane-interalated hybrid proteoglycants having heparan and chondroit sulfate chains on the same 40,000 core protein, and that the CPGIIB proteoglycain is a fibronectin receptor on the tumor cells.

the membrane-intercalated hybrid proteoglycane CPGIIIB, which is synthesized by a stroma-inducible clone of Lewis lung carcinoma, binds to fibronactin through its heparan sulfates and mediates the attachment of the tumor cells to interstitial matrix, thereby inducing the stroma formation.
CPGIIIM and CPGIIIT are membrane-intercalated core proteins, and CPGIIIB is a membrane-intercalating hybrid proteoglycane, all of which are derived from the same gene product.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a membrane-intercalating heparan sulfate proteoglycan can mediate the interaction between the cancer cells and interstitial matrices, thereby playing an essential role in cancer cell invasion and metastasis.
